title: The Chief of the Kus Police and the Sharper (हिन्दी)

keywords: the chief of the kus police and the sharper
full_text:
The Chief of Police of Qus in Upper Egypt had successfully captured many desert outlaws and river brigands, earning a reputation for unshakeable firmness. However, this success caused pride to take root in his chest, and he began to boast that no criminal in Egypt could escape his net.

A famous sharper of Cairo, passing through Qus, resolved to administer a gentle lesson in humility. He donned the robes of an affluent Syrian silk merchant, rented a fine house near the river, and deposited a heavy iron-bound chest in the police headquarters for safekeeping, claiming it contained ten thousand gold pieces.

The police chief locked the chest in his private treasury with three keys and treated the merchant with supreme deference.

Two weeks later, the sharper approached the chief in great distress: 'O Chief, I have received urgent letters from Damascus; I must travel immediately. Grant me my chest, and send four of your most trusted guards to accompany me to the boat on the Nile.'

The chief opened the treasury, watched the heavy chest loaded onto a cart, and dispatched four armed guards to escort the merchant to the river barge. As the boat cast off into the current, the sharper stood on the deck, waved politely to the guards, and shouted: 'Farewell, brave protectors! Be so kind as to open the chest in your treasury tomorrow and read the parchment I have left for your master!'

The puzzled guards ran back to the chief, who opened his treasury—only to find another identical chest sitting in the corner! Breaking open the locks, the chief found the chest filled with broken river cobblestones and a letter:

'O Chief of Qus, remember that he who believes he knows all the tricks of men is already half-deceived. While your guards were loading the heavy chest of stones onto the cart, my companion quietly carried the real treasure chest out through your back gate. Farewell, and remember that vigilance is a continuous duty, not a crown to rest upon.'

The police chief buried his face in his hands, laughing at his own folly, and never again boasted of his infallibility.
moral: True security comes from constant vigilance and humility, not overconfidence in past victories. [HI]
